name: Lithium manganese dioxide
electrolyte: Lithium salt in organic solvent (commonly lithium perchlorate in propylene carbonate and dimethoxyethane)
self_discharge: About 1% of capacity per year at room temperature (Energizer coin cells)
summary: Lithium manganese dioxide cells pair a lithium metal anode with a manganese dioxide cathode to give 3.0 V nominal from a single cell. They are the CR chemistry of the CR2032 coin cell and the CR123A photo battery, and Wikipedia puts them at about 80% of the lithium battery market.
body:
## How it works

A lithium manganese dioxide cell, IEC system C, pairs a lithium metal anode with a heat-treated manganese dioxide cathode. The electrolyte is a lithium salt in an organic solvent; Wikipedia gives lithium perchlorate in propylene carbonate and dimethoxyethane as common. Energizer writes the reaction as Li + Mn(IV)O2 → Mn(III)O2(Li+). In a coin cell the can is the positive terminal and the cap is the negative.

## Discharge behavior

Nominal voltage is 3.0 V and open-circuit voltage about 3.3 V. Energizer describes a relatively flat discharge curve until near end of life, followed by a quick drop that devices should be designed to handle. Internal resistance is high in small coin cells: Energizer gives about 10 Ω for a fresh 2032, against about 0.25 Ω for an AA alkaline, and resistance rises as the cell discharges. Inrush and pulse currents therefore cause voltage dips, and Energizer notes that a device with a cutoff above 2.0 V may leave significant capacity unused. Panasonic lists its standard CR2032 at 225 mAh, and its primary lithium catalog states nominal capacities to a 2.0 V cutoff at 20 °C.

Temperature ratings vary by product. Energizer gives −40 to 60 °C for its coin cells and −20 to 60 °C for its cylindrical cells; Panasonic rates standard CR coin cells from −30 to 85 °C and high-temperature types such as the CR2032A from −40 to 125 °C. Wikipedia lists 280 Wh/kg and 580 Wh/L. Coin cells stored at room temperature have a shelf life of 10 to 12 years and lose about 1% of capacity per year through vapor exchange at the seal; the escaping dimethoxyethane has an ether-like odor that Energizer says is not a safety concern.

## Uses

Coin cells in the CR2016, CR2025 and CR2032 family power key fobs, remote keyless entry, memory backup, sensors and other compact long-life devices, according to Energizer and Panasonic listings. Cylindrical cells such as the CR123A (IEC CR17345) serve what Energizer calls professional and industrial applications. Panasonic lists high-rate pulse discharge and low-temperature performance among CR series features, attributing the low-temperature performance to the manganese dioxide positive electrode.

## History

Energizer states that lithium coin cells were developed in the 1970s as a 3 V miniature source for low-drain and backup uses. Panasonic cites more than 40 years of development and manufacturing of its coin lithium cells.

## Status

Current. IEC 60086-1 lists system C at 3.0 V nominal with a 3.7 V maximum open-circuit voltage.
strengths: Relatively flat discharge until near end of life
About 1% capacity loss per year in storage
High-rate pulse and low-temperature performance (Panasonic CR series)
limitations: High internal resistance in small coin cells (about 10 Ω for a fresh 2032)
Sudden voltage drop at end of life
safety: Ingestion hazard: coin cells 20 mm or larger cause the most serious injuries, even when spent
Swallowed cells can burn through the esophagus lining in two hours
Contains lithium metal; it ships under the lithium metal battery rules (IATA PI 968 to 970)
